item.title: How to build great evals - part 5 Stop dumbing down the results from your beautiful, complex eval suite into one single score. This often happens because some senior wants a simplified number to make decisions. Happened to us in the early days of Gemini. And I see it happening with a lot of teams....
item.description:
作者：Madhu Guru 账号：@realmadhuguru 简介：Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
How to build great evals - part 5
Stop dumbing down the results from your beautiful, complex eval suite into one single score. This often happens because some senior wants a simplified number to make decisions. Happened to us in the early days of Gemini.
And I see it happening with a lot of teams.
This is the tyranny of the average. AI systems do not have a simple dimension of quality.
Imagine a model that goes from: 85% -> 89% on simple summarization 80% -> 85% on basic factual QA 70% -> 63% on complex financial analysis
A single score obscures the fact that the model got worse on your frontier use case.
The immediate reaction to this is to come up with a weighted score. The problem with this is that you have created false, mathematical procession around a judgment call.
So what should you do? - keep a prioritized list of your evals per the ladder we discussed in part 4 yesterday. - get people who can look at the details and don’t look for abstracted simplicity. - Understand all the critical eval results in depth, where they fail, where they shine and make a decision on whether your new AI system is better or worse for your users.
Next post tomorrow!
Drop your eval questions below and I will answer in future posts.
Share this with your teammates. And your managers who run from complexity.

item.description:
作者：Peter Yang 账号：@petergyang 简介：Practical AI tutorials and interviews for busy people | Get my best AI skills and guides at https://t.co/6VAA6p81x6
Instinct is very well done.
I'm particularly impressed by how smooth the onboarding experience is to connect iMessages, Google Workspace, and my MCPs. The best builder prioritize onboarding and new user needs :)
Instinct also feels more proactive than some of the other assistants - it'll suggest things it can do right away after connecting a MCP.
However, I can't see myself doing real work with Instinct since it's all just in one thread. This is the same issue I have with @bot, the UX is very clean but often I want to have multiple threads going with the same bot.
I think I'll use Instinct more as an assistant for random chores and tasks.
For actual work, I'm still sticking to ChatGPT Work and Codex.
P.S. I asked Instinct if I have any invites to give out and it says invites are paused, so don't ask me for any (yet) 🙂

item.title: What Chess.com Teaches US About Superhuman Capabilities, with CEO Erik Allebest
item.description:
播客：No Priors
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:24 COVID happened, Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, and we're like, oh, this might just be a flash in the pan, like treadmills and sourdough bread. But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the mittens bot and the cheating scandal. And we just spiked again. And then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline.
Speaker 2 | 00:24 - 00:29 How do you think about, like, how to design a rating system for poker?
Speaker 1 | 00:29 - 00:48 We're bringing the chess playbook, which is like, how good are you really? Not just can you buy the most chips or can you use a bot or can you steal the most money? Whatever it is, we've all played those games where you're playing for M and M's and someone's just, like, all in all the time and they just rebuy more M and M's. As people get used to, like, wait. I actually care about my poker rating.
Speaker 1 | 00:48 - 00:57 People are gonna care about it as much as money because it's a reflection of, like, the value and their skill as a player. I think this is gonna be quite an interesting innovation for for
Speaker 2 | 01:10 - 01:44 the chess.com domain out of bankruptcy auction in 2005 for $55 when almost every investor told him it was an uninvestable niche passion project. Two decades later, he's built the dominant chess platform with more than 250,000,000 members, 200,000,000 a year in revenue and a mission to get a billion people to play chess. It's a game that's more popular than ever, despite computers outclassing humans at it for the last thirty years. We talk about what AI means for games, the future of chess.com, how to build a rating system for poker and the future of human skills. Welcome, Eric.
Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:47 Eric, it's great to have you on No Priors. Welcome.
Speaker 1 | 01:47 - 01:49 Thank you so much for having me.
Speaker 2 | 01:49 - 02:05 So I'd love to just make sure our listeners have a little bit of the backstory of chess.com and how you built this business. But could you paint a little bit of a picture of just, you know, usage and both the company and the user base and product today first?
Speaker 1 | 02:05 - 02:25 Yeah, sure. We are we are much larger than I ever thought we would be. So it's kind of wild to say these numbers for me. We're about 10,000,000 daily active users, about 40 or 50,000,000 monthly active users. It's always a little slower in the summertime as people are, you know, in the, in the Northern Hemisphere out and about.
Speaker 1 | 02:26 - 02:55 We have more than two fifty million registered members and more revenue than I thought we would end up with as a chess company. A little, I think this year we'll do a little over 200,000,000, which is frankly, again, surprising. We have about six fifty people on our team who love chess, are passionate about the game, and are working hard to, you know, make our members happy and to grow the game, and to be the best possible place to work. Those are our three kind of the three areas of our mission.
Speaker 2 | 02:55 - 03:10 Amazing. And you took a, I guess, somewhat unconventional startup path or founder CEO path to get here. I'm certainly think of you as founder. What how did you end up owning the business?
Speaker 1 | 03:11 - 03:41 Well, we didn't start by owning a business. We just started by owning a domain name that we got from a bankruptcy auction in 2005. Someone else owned the domain name. They were building chess software, but they, you know, couldn't pay their, their debts and, and the money they'd raised a little bit of money to try to do that, and ended up with a failed business. And so, a friend and I bought the chess.com domain name for $56,000 and we were going to build a chess community.
Speaker 1 | 03:41 - 03:53 We wanted to be like MySpace and build a chess community where people could kind of come and, and and express themselves and learn and share. We bought the domain name and started building.
Speaker 2 | 03:53 - 04:00 And, we'll bridge the gap from that to the scale of community you have today. Like, how did you grow? How did you think about fundraising?
Speaker 1 | 04:01 - 04:16 Yeah. So, did think about fundraising. You know, obviously, I was at, I was at Stanford Business School at the time. So, you know, Sandhill Road was right there, and I had access to a lot of venture capitalists. They were, you know, teachers and guests in, you know, classrooms I was in.
Speaker 1 | 04:16 - 04:29 And so I had a lot of meetings and basically most of them said, this is uninvestable. You should get a real job. Don't waste your time with this. And so I wasn't able to raise any money. No one believed in the vision.
Speaker 1 | 04:29 - 04:42 I asked some classmates if they wanted to like join me on this venture. And they're like, nah, we're going go like do something serious. And, so then my friend and I, you know, he was kind of the CTO. I was the product person. Just the two of us started building it together.
Speaker 1 | 04:43 - 05:31 Didn't raise any money. Eventually I started putting money in. I had money from a, you know, a couple of previous businesses I had sold, borrowed like a little bit of money from my friend's mom, and then paid it back later, but, you know, we just really kind of grew at the speed of cash, and after we launched in 2007, right as I graduated, from school, and then I think within like eighteen months, we were starting to charge memberships for like online chess learning, and we pretty quickly became profitable, and then we just grew, you know, as we had more revenue, we would just hire somebody new, whether it was a community manager, a developer, a system, a SIS admin, you know, eventually designers. It just kind of grew as we had money to, you know, for it to grow. And we never then again considered raising money.
Speaker 1 | 05:31 - 05:46 It never crossed our minds. We just thought, Hey, we're profitable. Let's just keep, let's keep growing. And we always thought like, oh, when we hit like 50 people, like we're never going to have more than 50 people on our team. And of course we blew, we're never going to have more than a 100 people on our team.
Speaker 1 | 05:46 - 06:18 And then we just stopped saying that because, you know, chess just continued to surprise us as to how big it got. And it still surprises me. But what's interesting is now I'm like, if two fifty million people have said they want to play chess at some point on chess.com, like, why don't we have 50,000,000 daily active users? You know, a billion people should be playing chess. So now our ambitions are pretty big and we see the good that chess does in the world and brings people together and gives them confidence and, you know, teaches them that you never really lose if you learn.
Speaker 1 | 06:18 - 06:29 And it's a great game for learning and spending time. So now our mission is huge and we're like, we're going to be, you know, bigger than we are today. So we're quite excited about our mission.
Speaker 2 | 06:29 - 06:45 How did you think about competition and like the rate of growth you needed to have? Yeah. And how do you think about it today? Because there there are I don't know if you can say the words, but there are platforms like Leechess out there. Yeah.
Speaker 2 | 06:46 - 07:05 Amongst the many drivers of people raising a huge amount of capital, some businesses are more CapEx intensive than others. But even when they're not naturally. The desire to like be the dominant player in a market, way chess.com is right is, I think, a common driver.
Speaker 1 | 07:05 - 07:22 Yeah, and I think that's fair. And I want to give the caveat that the chess, you know, the chess industry, as we call it today, didn't exist, you know, twenty years ago. It was like some some apps and like one kind of, you know, a couple of players. There was free Internet c...
